San Telmo is the oldest and one of the most historically rich neighborhoods in Buenos Aires, Argentina, famous for its preserved colonial architecture, cobblestone streets, and pivotal role in the city's origins. Originally established around 1708 and named after Saint Pedro González Telmo, the patron saint of seafarers, this district transformed from an industrial and indigenous outpost into an elite residential area, and later a haven for European immigrants.

evidence.title: Evolution of the Neighborhood
evidence.snippet: Colonial Era & Indigenous Outpost: Before formal incorporation in 1708, the area was separated from central Buenos Aires by a ravine and inhabited largely by marginalized groups and the indigenous Querandí. Jesuits established a mission here before their expulsion in 1767.

evidence.title: Evolution of the Neighborhood
evidence.snippet: The Yellow Fever Turning Point: Wealthy families built grand Italianate mansions here in the mid-19th century. However, the devastating 1871 yellow fever epidemic forced wealthier residents to flee north to neighborhoods like Recoleta, leaving the grand mansions to be converted into multi-family conventillos for incoming European immigrants.

evidence.title: Evolution of the Neighborhood
evidence.snippet: Modern Preservation: Threatened by highway construction projects in the 1970s and 80s, the community fought back to preserve its architectural identity, cementing San Telmo as the bohemian, tango-infused conservation district it is today.
